learningObjective: Precisely define a basic block and identify what constitutes a valid CFG edge.
stem: Which statement correctly defines a basic block (BB) and the corresponding control-flow graph (CFG)?

options.text: A basic block is a maximal straight-line sequence of instructions with exactly one entry (the first instruction) and one exit (the last instruction, typically a branch or terminator); the CFG has an edge from BB_i to BB_j if control can flow from the terminator of BB_i to the entry of BB_j.
A basic block is any sequence of instructions with no data dependency between them; the CFG is a data-flow graph over these blocks.
A basic block is a function body; the CFG has one node per function and edges represent calls.
A basic block is a loop body; the CFG has one node per loop and edges represent nesting.

explanation: Textbook definition: a basic block is a maximal straight-line code sequence with a single entry (first instruction) and single exit (last instruction). CFG edges represent possible control flow between blocks (via branches, fall-throughs, and terminators). The other options misidentify BBs as data-flow constructs, functions, or loop bodies.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: canonical BB and CFG definition.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: BBs are defined by control flow (single entry/exit), not by data dependency.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: a function typically contains many BBs; a call graph is a different structure.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: a loop body typically contains multiple BBs; loops are structural properties of the CFG.

nonImplications: Does not imply that BBs cannot contain calls (they can, unless calls are treated as terminators for exception-safety analysis).
Does not imply the CFG is unique for a given program; different partitions may exist, but the maximal one is standard.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses control-flow with data-flow analysis units.
